extracted.intended_audience: editors, authors, and publishers preparing copy for the University of Chicago Press (and similar publishing contexts)
extracted.subtask_description: A publishing style manual focused on rules for capitalization, use of small capitals, italics, quotation marks, and spelling/numbering conventions for books, periodicals, and related printed matter. Guidance is aimed at preparing copy, bibliographies, addresses, headings, scientific names, quotations, and other common editorial elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-title capitalization (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: In foreign titles, in addition to capitalizing the first word, follow specific language-based rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See subrules for Latin, French/Italian/Spanish/Swedish/Norwegian, German/Danish, and Dutch specifics (42 a–d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin title capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In Latin titles, capitalize proper nouns and adjectives derived therefrom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: De amicitia, Bettum Gallicum. (42a)

rubrics_metrics.name: French/Italian/Spanish/Swedish/Norwegian title capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In these languages' titles, capitalize proper nouns but do not capitalize adjectives derived from proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Histoire de la litterature frangaise; Novelle e racconti popolari italiani; Antologia de poetas liricos castellanos; Svenska litteraturens historic. (42b)

rubrics_metrics.name: German and Danish title capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In German and Danish titles, capitalize all nouns but not adjectives, except German adjectives derived from personal names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Geschichte des deutschen Feudalwesens (but: die Homerische Frage); Videnskabens Fremskridt i detnittende Aarhundrede. Abbreviations like B.P.W. for Berliner philologische Wochenschrift. (42c)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dutch title capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In Dutch titles, capitalize all nouns and all adjectives derived from proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Geschiedenis der Nederlandsche Taal. (42d)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite article in titles of newspapers and periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, as a rule, treat the definite article as part of the title when mentioning newspapers, magazines, and similar publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'the Chicago Tribune', 'the School Review', 'the Annual Register of the University of Chicago.' (43)

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of ancient manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of ancient manuscripts and use MS (singular) or MSS (plural) as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Codex Bernensis, Cod. Canonicianus. (44)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenated compound capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Twentieth-Century Progress,' 'The Economy of High-Speed Trains.' Do not capitalize components that are not nouns: 'Fifty-first Street', 'Lives of Well-known Authors.' (45)

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-head capitalization rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In side-heads, do not capitalize any but the first word and proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See items 56 and 172 for related guidance. (45 note)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific Latin names capitalization (higher taxa)
rubrics_metrics.description: In botanical, geological, zoological, and paleontological matter, capitalize scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera; do not capitalize their English derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cotylosauria (but: cotylosaurs); Felidae (but: felids); Carnivora (but: carnivores). (46)

rubrics_metrics.name: Species names capitalization exception
rubrics_metrics.description: In botanical and zoological matter, names of species derived from persons or generic names may be capitalized; in geological and medical matter, names of species are never capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Cocos nucifera, Rosa Carolina; but geological: Pterygomatopus schmidti, Conodectus favosus. (46)

rubrics_metrics.name: Names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kafir, Negro (in ethnic sense), Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials. (47)

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical names capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical work, capitalize names of planetary bodies, stars, and star groups (but not generic words like 'sun', 'earth', 'moon', 'stars').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also capitalize designations from well-known catalogues and Flamsteed numbers: Saturn; Ursa Major; the Milky Way; M 13; Bond 619; N.G.C. 6165; 85 Pegasi. (48)

rubrics_metrics.name: University divisions/offices/courses capitalization (official)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University of Chicago in official work concerning administration or curricula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'the School of Education (the School)', 'Department of Anthropology (also: the Department)', 'the Board of Trustees (the Trustees, the Board)', 'Dean of the Faculties (also: the Faculty)'. (49)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of capitals and small capitals in letters (date, salutatory, signature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set names of town and state in the date line and salutatory phrase and the signature and residence in caps and small caps with specified alignment and indentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CHICAGO, ILL., January i, 1911; MY DEAR MR. SMITH:; CHARLES W. SCOTT. (50)

rubrics_metrics.name: WHEREAS / NOTE / SECTION formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words like 'WHEREAS' in resolutions, 'NOTE' in notes (not footnotes), and 'SECTION' introducing paragraphs in constitutions/by-laws set in capitals as prescribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NOTE. — It should be noticed that ...; SECTION 1. This association shall be styled ...; usual practice abbreviates 'SECTION' to 'SEC.' after first use. (51)

rubrics_metrics.name: Small capitals for A.M., P.M., B.C., A.D.
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M., P.M., B.C., and A.D. in small capitals without spaces between letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-case initial for formerly proper names and derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a small (lower-case) initial for words of common usage that originated as proper names and for their derivatives where the origin is now obscure; also generally for verbs derived from proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonanza, china, morocco, guinea-pig, boycott, roman (type), italicize, anglicize. (53)

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor literary-reference terms in lower case
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, set minor subdivisions and their abbreviations (chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note) in lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations: chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n. (54)

rubrics_metrics.name: Units of measurement abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard abbreviations for units of measurement (h.=hour, min.=minute, sec.=second; lb.=pound, oz.=ounce; yd.=yard, ft.=foot, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-head capitalization reiterated
rubrics_metrics.description: In side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See items 56 and references to 172 and 280 for related rules. (56)

rubrics_metrics.name: First word of connected quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quotation is immediately connected with the preceding text (through a conjunction or otherwise), capitalize the first word of the quotation even if it begins a sentence in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations and exception at items 35 and 131. (57)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of italics for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to which emphasis or special importance is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But beware excessive use; over-italicized pages are not pleasing and weaken emphasis. (58)

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics for foreign words and phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize foreign words or phrases inserted into English text that are not incorporated into English usage; also single sentences or brief passages in foreign language not long enough for reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung', 'Napoleon's coup d'etat'. Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of institutions/places whose English usage requires roman type; and do not italicize foreign words that are sufficiently anglicized. (59)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not italicize certain anglicized foreign words
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not italicize foreign words of everyday occurrence that have become sufficiently anglicized even if they retain accents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed (addendum, ensemble, clientele, etc.). Also do not hyphenate these foreign words when used as adjectives. (59 note)

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of publications in italics
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize titles of publications — books (including plays, essays, cycles of poems, single long poems, symphonies), pamphlets, treatises, periodicals, and names of journals when appearing in the journal itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer-Night's Dream; the Modern Language Review; the Chicago Tribune. Exception: may depart in lengthy bibliographical lists, tables, or where italics would be excessive. Books of the Bible and titles of ancient manuscripts set in roman. (60)

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics exception in bibliographical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not strictly require italics in lengthy bibliographical lists, tables, or other matter where italics would be overly prevalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See note to 41 and Botanical Gazette footnote practice. (60 note)

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin/technical abbreviations to italicize
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize certain words, phrases, and abbreviations used in literary and legal references (ad loc., circa (ca.), et al., ibid., idem, infra, loc. cit., op. cit., passim, sic, sc., supra, s.v., vide).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But do not italicize cf., e.g., i.e., v. or vs. (unless ambiguity results), viz., etc. (61)

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics for index cross-reference words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics (or differentiation) for words like 'See' and 'See also' in an index or similar compilation to separate them from context; likewise 'for' and 'read' in errata lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: See also Sociology; for levee read levee (with accent). (62)

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics in legal citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize the names of plaintiff and defendant in citation of legal causes and titles of proceedings containing prefixes like in re, ex parte, in the matter of, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Conolly v. Union Sewer Pipe Co.; In re Smith; Ex parte Brown; In the matter of the petition of Henry Robinson for a writ of habeas corpus. (63)

rubrics_metrics.name: Address-line formatting in speeches and letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Set address lines in speeches, reports, and primary address lines in letters flush, in a separate line with nouns capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen:; Mr. John Smith, 321 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill.; DEAR SIR: (64)

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting of position/title in signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: In signatures, set the position or title after the name; if one word, run into same line; if more than one word but no longer than the name, center the first letter under the name and indent one em on the right; if longer than the name, center the name over the second line and set that flush.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules subject to special-case exigencies. Examples given: ARTHUR P. MAGUIRE, Secretary; CARTER H. HARRISON Mayor of Chicago; CHARLES M. GAYLEY Professor of English Language and Literature. (65)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a), b), c) subdivisions and fractional letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a), b), c), etc., to indicate subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph, double parentheses if run in); use a, b, c affixed to verse/page numbers to denote fractional parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luke 4:3a. (66)

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters to designate unknown quantities and lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters to designate unknown quantities, lines, etc., in algebraic, geometrical, and similar matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ac+bc=c(a+b); lines ad and AD; the nth power. (67)

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters in legends referring to illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, italicize or use letters in legends or text referring to corresponding letters in accompanying illustrations whether or not they are italicized on the illustration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At the point A above (see diagram).' (68)

rubrics_metrics.name: References to particular letters formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to particular letters in roman: 'the letter u, a small v, a capital S.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize a letter used as a name placeholder or when only the initial is used with a dash or as a simple abbreviation. Examples: 'A bought land from B ...' 'General M'. (69)

rubrics_metrics.name: Shillings and pence abbreviations after numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 's.' and 'd.' (= shillings and pence) following numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 3s. 6d. (70)

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics for genera and species names together
rubrics_metrics.description: In zoological, geological, and paleontological matter, italicize Latin names of genera and species when used together, with the generic name in nominative singular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Rosa Carolina, Conodectes favosus, Phyteuma Halleri. (71)

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics for genera and species generally (botanical/paleontological)
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize names of genera and species when used together, and genera when used alone in botanical, geological, and paleontological matter; in medical matter, generally set such names in roman, avoiding italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Acer saccharum, Basidiobolus, Alternaria; medical practice: roman. (71)

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical/astrophysical italic rules (letters and catalog initials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics for lower-case Fraunhofer line letters, lower-case Baeyer letters for certain stars, and italics for initials used as titles of catalogues when not designating a particular celestial object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a, b, g, h; f Tauri, u Herculis; B.D., N.G.C. (71 a–c)

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical element symbols not italicized
rubrics_metrics.description: Use roman (not italics) for symbols of chemical elements (H, Ca, Ti).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not italicize Fraunhofer capital letters, spectral type letters, and H+Greek-letter combos
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern practice: do not use italics for Fraunhofer capital letters for spectral lines, letters designating spectral types of stars, or H with Greek letters used to designate hydrogen lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A-H, K; As, G2, Mb; Ha, H/?, etc. (71 note)

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize 'Resolved' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions, italicize the word 'Resolved.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Continued' after headlines or titles
rubrics_metrics.description: After headlines or titles, as a rule, use the word 'Continued'; at the end of articles use 'To be continued'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: THE SCOPE OF SOCIOLOGY— Continued; [To be continued]. (73)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotation marks for run-in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put between quotation marks (roman-quote) citations run into the text of a passage from an author in his own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short citations that are incorporated into the text should be in quotation marks and roman type. (74)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for consecutive quotations from different sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks when quotations from different authors or different works by the same author follow each other uninterrupted by original matter or by references to sources (except footnote figures), even if reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for words followed by definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Place between quotation marks a word or phrase accompanied by its definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Drop-folio' means a page-number at the foot of the page. (76)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for unusual/technical/ironical words
rubrics_metrics.description: Put unusual, technical, ironical, etc. words or phrases in quotation marks whether or not accompanied by a directing word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Her 'five o'clocks' were famous; She was wearing a gown of 'lobster-colored' silk. (77)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for translations
rubrics_metrics.description: In translations, enclose the English equivalent of a foreign word, phrase, or passage in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weltanschauung, 'world-view' or 'fundamental aspect of life'; Mommsen, Rimische Geschichte ('History of Rome'). (78)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for particular/ unusual words being referenced
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks around the particular or unusual word(s) to which attention is directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; the name 'Chicago'. Do not use when discussing words/terms with clear meaning (e.g., The definition of the word God). (79)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for book-series titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Place titles of book series in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'English Men of Letters Series'; 'International Critical Commentary'. (80)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for shorter poem titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of shorter poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shelley's 'To a Skylark.' (81)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for cited titles of subdivisions and short works
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for cited titles of subdivisions (parts, books, chapters), papers, lectures, sermons, articles, toasts, mottoes, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: chap. ii, 'John Stuart Mill'; articles 'Cross', 'Crucifixion'. Note: references to Preface, Introduction, Table of Contents, Index of a specific work should be set with capitals without quotation marks. (82)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for names of ships
rubrics_metrics.description: Put names of ships in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the U.S. SS. 'Oregon'. (83)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclose titles of pictures and works of art in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Murillo's 'The Holy Family.' (84)

rubrics_metrics.name: Set long quotations in smaller type
rubrics_metrics.description: Set in smaller type ordinarily all prose extracts that will make five or more lines in the smaller type and all poetry citations of two lines or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An isolated prose quotation may be run into text if organically related; a 1–2 line quotation near longer reduced excerpts may be reduced for uniform appearance. (85)

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-size reduction guidance for reduced citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce point size for reduced citations: from n pt. and 10 pt. to 9 pt., from 9 pt. to 8 pt., from 8 pt. to 6 pt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks should be omitted for reduced citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced citations should not have quotation marks, except in cases like consecutive quotations (see 75); as a rule, quotation marks should not be used with italics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks should include ellipses and 'etc.' when omitting material
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should always include ellipses and the phrase 'etc.' when otherwise it would not be clear they stand for omitted matter; perfect clearness case-by-case is the best criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate placement of 'etc.' inside or outside quotes to show whether it stands for omitted material in the quotation or not. (88)

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat quotation marks for broken-up quoted prose
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoted prose (matter set with quotation marks) is broken into paragraphs, repeat the quotation marks at the beginning of each paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear/align quotation marks for alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: When alignment is desired, quotation marks should be 'cleared' (project beyond line of alignment) so the body lines up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided showing cleared quotes at line left for alignment effect. (90)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use double and single quotation marks by nesting level
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double quotation marks for primary quotations, single for a quotation within a quotation, alternating back to double for a third, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate nested quoting conventions. (91)

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out titles of honor and forms of address preceding names
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out all religious, civil, and military titles of honor and respect and forms of address preceding the name, except Mr., Messrs., Mrs., Dr., Rev., Hon., St.; abbreviate Esq. following the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not set 'the Rev.' and 'the Hon.' except in quotations and correspondence. (92)

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out Christian names and 'von' as part of names
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out Christian (given) names (George, Charles, John) rather than abbreviations (Geo., Chas., Jno.), except where abbreviated forms appear in quoted matter or original signatures; also spell out 'von' as part of a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References in text (not parenthetical or footnote citations) to chapters, pages, etc., should also be spelled out (see 69). (93)

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out numbers under certain conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to exceptions, in ordinary reading-matter spell out all numbers of less than three digits unless statistical/technical or in groups of six or more following each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided; treat connected groups consistently and use figures if the largest contains three or more digits. (94)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures for decimals, degrees, dimensions, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, use figures for decimals, degrees, dimensions, distances, enumerations, money, percentage, weights, and similar technical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 10°, 45 miles, 3 cubic feet, 24 pages, 100 bushels, 9 per cent, 45 pounds, $1,000. (94 note)

rubrics_metrics.name: Round numbers phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Express approximate round numbers in spelled-out even units (unit = 100 for numbers < 1000, unit = 1000 for numbers >= 1000), unless more precise figure is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'five hundred' (but 'at 550'); 'a thesis of about three thousand words' (but 'about 2,700'). Use 'fifteen hundred' not 'one thousand five hundred' if spelled out. (95)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start sentences with numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, however high, and all abbreviated terms of measurement or number should be spelled out when beginning a sentence; reconstruct sentence if impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women...' When impracticable, rewrite: 'The total number ... was 593 men.' (96)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sums of money in ordinary reading-matter spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of money occurring in isolated ordinary reading-matter should be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The admission was two dollars.' In close enumerations or statistical contexts use figures: 'Admission: men, $2; women, $1; children, 25 cents.' (97)

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of day phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter, express times of day in words (at four; at half-past two in the afternoon; at seven o'clock); in statistical/enumerative contexts and with A.M./P.M. use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example statistically: at 4:15 P.M. (omit 'o'clock' in such connections). (98)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ages wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Express ages in words where appropriate: 'eighty years and four months old'; 'children between six and fourteen.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers for centuries, dynasties, sessions, military bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out numbers for centuries, Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, military bodies, political divisions, thoroughfares, and similar cases unless brevity is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, second session; Fifth Avenue. (100)

rubrics_metrics.name: Decade references phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to particular decades in words: 'in the nineties.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of months spelled out except in statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out names of months except in statistical matter or long enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from January 1 to April 15 (omit st, d, th after dates). (102)

rubrics_metrics.name: United States style exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'United States' spelled out except in quotations and certain connections (e.g., General Schofield, U.S.A.; U.S. SS. 'Oregon'); in footnotes and similar references, use U.S. Geological Survey etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Railroad / Fort / Mount / Port capitalization in geographic names
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out 'Railroad' (not R.R. or Ry.), and capitalize 'Fort', 'Mount', and 'Port' in geographical appellations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad; Fort Wayne; Mount Elias; Port Huron. (104)

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of publications ordinarily spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, spell out names of publications; this rule is modifiable for expediency, authoritative usage, or author preference—if in doubt, spell out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good taste condones spelling-out offenses more readily than the opposite. (105)

rubrics_metrics.name: State abbreviations following towns
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviate names of states, territories, and possessions following those of towns using standard abbreviations without spaces between letters in lists, signatures, bibliographical matter, but not ordinarily in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table of standard abbreviations is provided (Ala., Alaska, Ariz., etc.). (106)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate Company/Brothers and ampersand in technical/bibliographic matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnote references, bibliographies), abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use '&' (ampersand) in names of commercial firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Macmillan Co., Macmillan & Co., Harper Bros.; Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad. In nontechnical running text, 'Company' and 'Brothers' may be spelled out. When firm name does not consist of proper names, spell out 'and' (American Steel and Wire Co.). (107)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate 'Saint' before place names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'St.' for 'Saint' or 'Saints' before place names: St. Louis, St. Peter's Church, SS. Peter and Paul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, omit 'St.' in connection with apostles, evangelists, church fathers in running text: Luke, Paul, Augustine (not St. Luke, St. Paul). (108–109)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations for Bible books and versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard abbreviations for books of the Bible, Apocrypha, Apocalyptic material, and common versions (e.g., Gen., Matt., Ps., A.V., R.V., LXX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full tables and lists provided for Old Testament, New Testament, Apocrypha, and versions. In running text do not abbreviate references to whole books or chapters: 'The story is presented in Revelation, chapter 10.' (109 continued)

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetical abbreviations for volumes, numbers, pages, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: In parenthetical literary references, footnotes, and bibliographic matter, abbreviate volume, number, psalm, division, chapter, article, section, page, column, verse, line, note, figure with standard abbreviations (Vol., No., Ps., Div., chap., art., sec., p., col., vs., l., n., Fig.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pp., pp. ff., pp. sff., ed. (d) as appropriate; conventions for ranges and continuations are specified. (109 continued)

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric system and common measurement abbreviations after numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use common designations and symbols for metric and other standard measurements following numerals: m., dm., cm., mm., c.m. (=cubic meter), sq. mi., gm. (=gram), gr. (=grain), h. (=hour), min. (=minute), sec. (=second), lb. (=pound), oz., yd., ft., in., kg., kw., mg., mag. (=magnitude), A (=angstrom), h.p. (=horse-power), C. (=Centi-grade), F. (=Fahrenheit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 123 for related guidance. (109 continued)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard abbreviations for electrical engineering values
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the recommended standard abbreviations for electrical and technical values (a-c., b.h.p., B.t.u., c-p., cm., cir. mils, e.h.p., e.m.f., ft., gal., gm., hr., in., i.h.p., kg., km., kw., watt-hr., yd., etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table of abbreviations provided and note about hyphenated abbreviations: the first element does not take a period. (109 continued)
